core.text: Add *-ns* to a verb's stem and you get an adjective: **the present participle (the '-ing' word that describes a noun)**. *dormīre* (to sleep) → *dormiēns* (sleeping); *canere* (to sing, crow) → *canēns*; *vigilāre* (to be awake) → *vigilāns*. It describes a noun and agrees with it, taking the 3rd-declension endings on the stem *-nt-*: *puer dormiēns* (the sleeping boy), *puerum dormientem*, *puerī dormientis*, *puerōs dormientēs*. Latin name: participium praesentis.
A participle is a verb used like an adjective: *the fleeing soldiers*, *a boy sleeping in bed*. An *-ing* word used as a noun (*sleeping is pleasant*) is a gerund.
Stem + -ns (genitive -ntis): -āns, -ēns, -ēns, -iēns by conjugation; agrees with its noun like a 3rd-declension adjective.

invented.en: The mother hears her daughter singing.

core.text: Both come out as *-ing* in English. The participle ends in *-ns / -nt-* and describes a noun that is doing something: *puer dormiēns*. The gerund (the '-ing' noun form: ad bibendum = for drinking) ends in *-nd-* and names the action itself: *ad dormiendum* — for sleeping. *-nt-* = someone doing it; *-nd-* = the doing.

teach.title: What it does
teach.say: Take a verb and turn it into a word that describes a noun, and you have **the present participle (the '-ing' word that describes a noun)**. *puer dormiēns* is 'the sleeping boy', or 'the boy, sleeping'. It does two things at once: it keeps the verb's meaning and it agrees with its noun the way any adjective does.

check.ask: Which word is the participle, and which noun is it describing?

teach.title: How it is built: -āns from the 1st conjugation
teach.say: One cell. A 1st-conjugation verb — the *-āre* kind — makes its present participle in *-āns*: *cantāre* → *cantāns* (singing), *portāre* → *portāns* (carrying), *ambulāre* → *ambulāns* (walking).

teach.title: -ēns and -iēns from the others
teach.say: One cell more, on a different verb. The 2nd and 3rd conjugations make *-ēns*: *vidēre* → *vidēns*, *dūcere* → *dūcēns*. The 4th conjugation and the *-iō* verbs of the 3rd make *-iēns*: *audīre* → *audiēns*, *dormīre* → *dormiēns*, *fugere* → *fugiēns*.

teach.title: The stem is -nt-
teach.say: *-ns* is the form for the subject, and for a neuter noun the object as well (*animal dormiēns* either way). Every other form is built on *-nt-*, with the endings of a 3rd-declension adjective: the accusative (the object form) *-ntem* (*fugientem*), the genitive (the 'of' form) *-ntis* (*plōrantis*), the dative (the 'to/for' form) *-ntī* (*dormientī*), the plural *-ntēs* (*currentēs*) and the neuter plural *-ntia* (*dormientia*). The table shows those endings on an ordinary 3rd-declension adjective.

show.say: brevem / brevis — the -ntem and -ntis of the participle are these endings

check.ask: Fill the accusative (the object form) and the genitive (the 'of' form) of *brevis* — the endings the participle borrows.

teach.title: Telling it from the sentence's own verb
teach.say: Both come from the same verb, so look at the ending. A participle ends in *-ns* or *-nt-* and belongs to a noun: *frātrem dormientem*, the sleeping brother. The sentence's own verb carries a person ending: *Quīntus dormit*, Quintus is sleeping. A participle can never be the only verb in a sentence.

check.ask: *cantāns* and *cantat* come from one verb. Which is the participle, and which is the sentence's own verb?

teach.title: Using it: make it agree
teach.say: Find the noun the participle describes and copy its case, number and gender. In *Iūlius puerōs in hortō lūdentēs spectat* the boys are the object, plural and masculine, so the participle is *lūdentēs* — not *lūdēns*, which would describe Julius.

check.ask: Mīles fortis hostēs ___ petit. *hostēs* is plural and it is the object. (fugiō)

more.text: The ablative singular is *-e* when the participle works as a verb (*ā puerō dormiente*, and in the ablative absolute), but *-ī* when it has become a plain adjective (*ā patre amantī*, *sapientī*). The genitive plural is *-ium*, the neuter plural *-ia*: *animālia volantia* — flying animals.

It keeps its verb-power and can have an object: *gallum canentem audit* — he hears the cock crowing. The present participle means *at the same time as the main verb*, whatever that tense is: *puer dormiēns gallum nōn audīvit* — while he was sleeping he did not hear. Some participles have turned into ordinary adjectives or nouns: *sapiēns* (wise), *parēns* (parent), *oriēns* (the east, where the sun is rising).

The learner's notes (week 14): the active participle adds *-(e)ns* to the stem; the *e* drops after *a-* and *e-*stems (*ambulāns, vidēns*) and stays in consonant, *-iō* and *i-*stems (*frangēns, percutiēns, veniēns*); every other form adds *-(e)nt-* plus a 3rd-declension ending, agreeing in case, number and gender; a participle may take an object or a phrase to form a participial phrase (*the soldiers fleeing from the battlefield*). Ørberg (chapter XIV): *vigilāns, iacēns, canēns, dormiēns* are participles, adjectives of the 3rd declension with genitive *-antis / -entis* and ablative *-e* or *-ī*.
